title: Memory Forensics with Volatility 3
description: Students install Volatility 3, download a publicly available memory dump from a simulated Windows compromise, run memory analysis plugins to enumerate processes and network connections, identify signs of malware injection, dump the suspicious process for further analysis, and document their findings in an IR-style artifact report.
objective: Students will use Volatility 3 to perform a structured memory forensics investigation on a captured RAM dump, identify a Cobalt Strike-style beacon through process and network analysis, detect code injection via malfind, extract the malicious payload, and produce an artifact summary suitable for inclusion in an incident report.

steps.title: Install Volatility 3 and Download Practice Memory Sample
steps.instructions:
Set up the Volatility 3 analysis environment and obtain a sample memory dump.

**Install Python 3 and Volatility 3:**
```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/volatilityfoundation/volatility3.git
cd volatility3

# Install dependencies
pip3 install -r requirements.txt

# Verify installation
python3 vol.py -h
```

**Download a practice memory sample:**

Option A — MemLabs Challenge 1 (recommended for beginners):
```
https://github.com/stuxnet999/MemLabs/tree/master/Lab%201
```

Option B — Use the course-provided sample from the resources portal: `memdump-lab05.raw`

**Download Windows symbol packs** (required for accurate results):
```bash
# Create symbols directory
mkdir -p volatility3/symbols

# Download from:
# https://downloads.volatilityfoundation.org/volatility3/symbols/
# Place ntsymbols_x64.zip in the symbols folder and extract
```

**Verify your dump file:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw banners.Banners
# Should output the Windows version string from the dump
```

steps.title: Enumerate Running Processes and Identify Anomalies
steps.instructions:
Run process enumeration plugins to build a picture of what was running at the time of capture.

**Step 1: List all processes linearly:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.pslist.PsList
```
Record: PID, PPID, process name, number of handles, start time.

**Step 2: View process tree to spot parent-child anomalies:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.pstree.PsTree
```

**Red flags to look for in the process tree:**
- `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe` spawned by `winword.exe`, `excel.exe`, or `outlook.exe`
- `svchost.exe` without `services.exe` (PID 644/692) as parent
- Processes running from unusual paths: `%TEMP%`, `%APPDATA%`, `C:\Users\Public\`
- Duplicate process names (two `lsass.exe`)
- Short-lived or recently terminated processes

**Step 3: Check command line arguments for suspicious flags:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.cmdline.CmdLine
```
Look for: base64-encoded `-enc` PowerShell, unusual wscript.exe arguments, download cradles.

**Document your findings:** In a text file, note every suspicious process with PID, parent PID, path, and your suspicion reasoning.

steps.title: Analyse Network Connections from Memory
steps.instructions:
Examine all network connections recorded in the memory dump to identify C2 communication.

**Run the network connections plugin:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.netstat.NetStat
```

**Output fields to analyse:**
- `Offset` — memory offset
- `Proto` — TCP/UDP
- `LocalAddr` / `LocalPort`
- `ForeignAddr` / `ForeignPort` — the remote host and port
- `State` — ESTABLISHED, LISTENING, CLOSED
- `PID` / `Owner` — which process owns this connection

**Suspicious indicators:**
- External connections on ports: `4444`, `1337`, `8080`, `8443`, `443` (to unknown IP)
- A process like `notepad.exe` or `explorer.exe` with an established TCP connection to an external IP
- Connections to Tor exit nodes or Bulletproof hosting (check IP on AbuseIPDB)
- `CLOSE_WAIT` state with an external IP (session was established recently)

**Enrich suspicious IPs:**
```bash
# Using curl to check AbuseIPDB
curl -G https://api.abuseipdb.com/api/v2/check \
  --data-urlencode "ipAddress=<SUSPICIOUS_IP>" \
  -H "Key: YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" | python3 -m json.tool
```

**Document:** Record the suspicious connection (process name, PID, foreign IP, port, state) — this is a key IOC for your incident report.

steps.title: Detect Code Injection with Malfind
steps.instructions:
Run the malfind plugin to find processes with executable memory regions that suggest code injection.

**Run malfind:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.malfind.Malfind 2>/dev/null | head -100
```

**Understanding malfind output:**
```
PID  Process    Start      End        Tag Hits  Protect
1234 svchost.exe 0x00ef0000 0x00efffff VadS  1   PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE

Hexdump:
4d 5a 90 00 03 00 00 00  04 00 00 00 ff ff 00 00  MZ..............
```

**Key flags for malicious injection:**
- `PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE` (RWX) — writable and executable simultaneously (abnormal)
- `MZ` (0x4D 0x5A) in the first bytes = PE file header — a DLL or EXE injected into memory
- Region is not mapped to any file on disk (private memory)

**Filter to a specific PID to reduce noise:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.malfind.Malfind --pid <SUSPICIOUS_PID>
```

**Cross-check with psscan to find hidden processes:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.psscan.PsScan
# Compare with pslist output — processes in psscan but not pslist = hidden
```

**Document:** Note the PID, process name, memory region start address, permission flags, and first 16 bytes of the injected region.

steps.title: Dump the Suspicious Process and Verify the Payload
steps.instructions:
Extract the suspicious process binary from memory for offline analysis.

**Create an output directory:**
```bash
mkdir -p extracted_files
```

**Dump the suspicious process executable and memory:**
```bash
# Dump process executable file
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.dumpfiles.DumpFiles \
  --pid <SUSPICIOUS_PID> \
  --dump-dir ./extracted_files/
```

**Alternatively, dump the specific injected region:**
```bash
python3 vol.py -f memdump-lab05.raw windows.memmap.MemMap \
  --pid <SUSPICIOUS_PID> \
  --dump
```

**Calculate the hash of extracted files:**
```bash
# Linux/Mac
sha256sum extracted_files/*.dmp

# Windows PowerShell
Get-FileHash extracted_files\*.dmp -Algorithm SHA256
```

**Submit the hash to VirusTotal:**
```bash
# Using curl (requires free VT API key)
curl -s -X POST "https://www.virustotal.com/vtapi/v2/file/report" \
  -d "apikey=YOUR_KEY&resource=<SHA256_HASH>"
```

**Write your final findings document:**
```
Suspicious Process Summary
==========================
PID:        <value>
Process:    <value>
Path:       <value>
Parent PID: <value>
Network:    <foreign IP>:<port> ESTABLISHED
Injection:  RWX region at <address>, MZ header found
Hash:       <SHA256>
VT Result:  <N>/70+ detections (e.g. Cobalt Strike, Meterpreter)
ATT&CK:     T1055 - Process Injection, T1071.001 - C2 over HTTP
```

Submit this file alongside your Volatility screenshots as your lab evidence.

expected_output: Students submit: (1) text file with process anomaly findings from pstree, (2) screenshot of netstat output highlighting the C2 connection, (3) screenshot of malfind output showing MZ header in injected memory, (4) SHA-256 hash of the dumped process, (5) VirusTotal screenshot showing detections for the dumped file, (6) completed findings summary document in the provided template format.
